translations: When Zhu Yingtai first asked her father to let her go to school, he assumed she was just complaining that the family library was too small.
"I’ll have someone buy a few more scrolls," her father said.
"Buying more books just means more books. I want to go to the academy, listen to the master teach, and debate with others."

Her father set down his teacup. In his eyes, sending a daughter away to study was less realistic than expecting the osmanthus tree in the courtyard to pack its bags and move house on its own. He cited the long distance, the dangers of the road, and the fact that the academy only accepted male students. Though her mother knew her daughter was bright, she also worried that such a journey would invite gossip.

Zhu Yingtai didn’t cry or beg. Instead, she reviewed several old books for her father and asked the family tutor to give her a test. When he questioned her on classical texts, she answered point by point; when he asked about mathematics, she used the family’s grain accounts to demonstrate; and when he asked how she would care for herself on a long trip, she listed her clothing, travel funds, lodging plans, and expected return date.
Her father still shook his head. "The academy’s rules won’t change just because you give good answers."
"If the rules won’t change, I can change my appearance."

Zhu Yingtai brought out a set of men’s clothes she had prepared long ago. Binding her hair, changing her robes, and adjusting her manners and speech wasn’t about making a fool of anyone; it was about crossing the threshold that barred girls from entering. Seeing that she had even prepared appropriate shoes, her father realized this idea hadn’t just popped up at the dinner table.
"What if you’re discovered?"
"I’ll follow the academy’s rules and avoid trouble. If I truly can’t continue, I’ll come back."
"What if you have to share a room with someone?"
"I’ll arrange things carefully."
"What if—"
Zhu Yingtai cut in, "If you keep asking, the academy will probably have to close for the season before I even leave."

Her mother couldn’t help but laugh, though her father kept a straight face. After the laughter subsided, Zhu Yingtai solemnly promised to send letters on schedule, return home after her studies, and not drag others into her secret. She made it clear that dressing as a man was merely a method to get an education, not an invitation to go out and play games.

Her father asked her to live at home in men’s clothes for a few days to see if she slipped up. Zhu Yingtai carried water, received visitors, and discussed books with the tutor, gradually becoming more natural. Once, a servant called out "Miss," and she immediately coughed loudly. The servant corrected himself to "Young Master," but because he changed his tone too loudly, he ended up calling everyone in the courtyard to come see the new young master.

The next day, her father arranged for an unsuspecting distant relative to visit, deliberately leaving Zhu Yingtai alone in the front hall to host him. As soon as the relative entered, he asked how Miss Zhu had been. Zhu Yingtai’s hand paused for only a split second as she poured tea, then she replied, "My older sister is studying in the inner courtyard. She’s annoyed that I used her inkstone to serve guests, and she asked me to send her regards to Uncle." With that, she set the teacup down steadily, without glancing behind the curtain.
As expected, the relative turned and asked, "Which young master of the Zhu family are you? Why haven’t I seen you before?"

"I wasn’t diligent in my studies before, so Father was too embarrassed to introduce me," Zhu Yingtai answered with complete seriousness. Behind the curtain, her mother nearly burst out laughing and had to cover her mouth with a handkerchief. Her father, however, frowned. After the guest left, he asked, "Why make jokes at your own expense?" Zhu Yingtai loosened her tight cuffs. "If a suddenly appeared distant cousin was perfect in every way, people would ask more questions. By admitting one trivial flaw first, people get busy believing that instead."

Her father didn’t praise her; he simply handed her a paper listing daily academy routines: morning classes, study partners, borrowing books, bathing, and evening roll calls. He asked her to explain how she would handle each situation. When she reached the part about sharing a room at night, she first proposed living in a small private room. Her father said if no such room was available, she should claim she was a light sleeper who needed to wake up early to fetch water, thus staying in a room near the entrance. Her mother listened for a while and reminded her, "Your plan can’t rely entirely on lies; it must rely on knowing your limits. When others respect you, you must not exploit that respect to tease them."

Zhu Yingtai nodded solemnly. She wasn’t practicing how to fool everyone around her, but how to protect her classmates while hiding her identity. She shortened the sashes that were likely to give her away and learned to secure her hair crown herself. The first time, she tied it too tight, and by midday, a red mark had formed on her forehead. When a servant asked, "Did Young Master solve a difficult problem?" she looked in the mirror and said, "This problem is called 'hair crown.' The answer is to loosen it by half an inch."

By the third day, people in the courtyard no longer loudly corrected themselves every time they saw her. Some handed her water, others discussed accounts, treating her like any other young man out studying. Her father observed for a long time and finally realized that his daughter hadn’t just prepared a set of men’s clothes; she had seriously thought through how to handle questioning, accidents, and kindness. His permission still came with difficulty, but it was no longer just a soft-hearted concession to a plea.

Zhu Yingtai said, "Let’s be more natural from now on. If a secret relies on the whole family reminding everyone to keep it quiet, it will spread through the neighborhood before we even reach the gate."

If a secret relies on the whole family reminding everyone to keep it quiet, it will spread through the neighborhood before we even reach the gate." Her father then had the accountant deliberately come to ask about an old debt, wanting to see if she would panic when dealing with an outsider. The accountant held a thin stack of ledgers, his brows slightly furrowed, as if trying to hide a major issue within a minor one. Zhu Yingtai first raised her hand to gently brush the dust off the ledgers, then answered in a gentle but firm tone, "The grain and rice accounts are clear. There’s nothing to worry about." Upon hearing this, the accountant’s lips curled up slightly, as if he’d heard a joke but dared not laugh out loud. He then pushed the ledgers onto the table, frowned deeply, and began to carefully check every figure. Zhu Yingtai glanced sideways at her father, a subtle smile flashing in her eyes, as if to say, "Don’t take it so seriously; even accounting can be relaxed." The accountant suddenly frowned, picked up his pen, and wrote a March entry into the April column, like a child’s homework being corrected into an adult’s mistake. Zhu Yingtai immediately countered, "What kind of revision is this? How can a March account be written into April?" The accountant was stunned, his pen hovering in mid-air. He hurriedly went back to recalculate, his brows knitted tight, as if blocked by an invisible wall. Her father stood by, his expression heavy, silent for half a day, before finally saying, "The outfit looks like a scholar’s, but the accounting looks more like your mother’s."
From behind the curtain, her mother replied, "If she really were like me, you would have agreed by now."

After a few days of testing, her father finally agreed. He prepared her travel documents and tuition fees, though he repeated his warnings over and over. Her mother sewed her pockets, hiding a small piece of old family cloth in the inner layer, reminding her that no matter how she dressed, she must still take care of herself.

On the morning of her departure, Zhu Yingtai tightened her hair crown one last time in front of the mirror. Wearing men’s clothes didn’t make her a different person, nor did her identity limit her desire for knowledge. As she stepped out of the house, she turned back to bow to her parents, then continued along the road to the academy.

She did not yet know who she would meet on the road, nor did she know that this pursuit of learning would lead to a bond that would span several years, eventually colliding with a marriage contract and social laws that could not be easily changed.
On the third day of the journey to the academy, mountain rain soaked the path.

Zhu Yingtai took shelter from the rain in an old pavilion and found that the bottom of her book bundle had already gotten wet. As she was untying it to rewrap it, a young scholar ran in, clutching his own scrolls. He pointed to the driest spot and offered it to her.
"I am Liang Shanbo, also heading to the academy," the scholar said.

Zhu Yingtai gave her name, pronouncing "Zhu Yingtai" as if it were an ordinary man’s name. Seeing her bundle was loose, Liang Shanbo helped find some dry straw to prop up the books. Together, they protected the books and waited for the rain to ease before continuing.

Ahead, a wooden bridge had been washed askew by the water, leaving only a narrow section passable. Liang Shanbo went first to test the bridge, but halfway across, he turned back. "The bridge can be crossed, and so can we. But if both our books fall into the water, the master will probably have to teach fish how to read first."

Zhu Yingtai split their luggage, and they each carried half, crossing one by one. When it was Liang Shanbo’s turn, a plank under his foot wobbled. Zhu Yingtai reached out and grabbed his bundle. The books didn’t fall, but Liang Shanbo ended up hugging the bridge pillar for a moment.
"Brother Liang, are you thanking the bridge?"
"I’m confirming whether it has any second thoughts."

This minor scare brought the two closer. As they walked and discussed their studies, Zhu Yingtai’s insights were quick and sharp, while Liang Shanbo was honest and kind. When Liang Shanbo asked how many brothers she had, she carefully answered that she was one of the older children and had sisters at home, then steered the conversation back to the master’s writings, keeping the question from probing too close to her identity.

Aman happened to be resting by the roadside. Seeing the two scholars debating as they walked, he took out his green bamboo slips to record the scene. Hearing Zhu Yingtai say, "Brother Liang, if you hadn’t looked back just now, the bridge would have taught you a lesson in swimming," he wrote down: "Upon first meeting, they advised each other to study. The curriculum includes falling into water."
